name: Anterior platysmaplasty

lead: Anterior platysmaplasty is a cosmetic neck-surgery technique. Through a small incision under the chin, the surgeon brings the inner edges of the platysma muscle together in the midline to reduce vertical bands and tighten the neck.

The appearance payoff is a cleaner angle between chin and neck and a more defined jawline. It is done alone or with a facelift, often together with removal of fat under the chin. Surgical series report improvement in cervicomental angle grade in most patients.

paras: It is performed by a plastic or facial plastic surgeon, usually combined with submental liposuction or lipectomy and often as part of a facelift or neck lift. Recovery involves swelling and bruising.

Reported risks include hematoma (the most common facelift complication), contour irregularities, limited lateral advancement, nerve or numbness effects and recurrence of bands. Choice of technique depends on skin laxity and fat location.

angle.text: The procedure directly alters neck contour by tightening the platysma, creating a cleaner cervicomental angle and more defined jaw-neck line.

lead: Anterior platysmaplasty, also called medial or corset platysmaplasty, is a surgical technique in which the platysma muscle is approached through an incision under the chin and its inner edges are brought together in the midline to reduce vertical banding.[1] It is used to improve neck contour and jawline definition, either alone or with a facelift.[1][2]

A 2005 paper described an 'anterior-only' approach in which 33 patients with mild to severe cervicomental angle deformities were treated with anterior platysmaplasty and submental lipectomy; 61 percent improved by one grade and 36 percent by two grades.[3]
In facelift surgery it has been used for decades but is reported to limit lateral advancement and may cause contour irregularities, leading to comparison with radiofrequency-assisted liposuction.[4]

paras: Medial platysmaplasty brings the inner muscle edges together through an incision under the chin; lateral platysmapexy instead supports the muscle at the sides, and the two can be combined. One study found medial platysmaplasty generally more effective than lateral pulling alone for midline deformity.[1]

In the 2005 anterior-only approach, patients with obtuse angles and good skin elasticity may be treated with liposuction alone, those with subplatysmal fat or mild to moderate laxity with anterior lipectomy and platysmaplasty, and those with marked skin excess with a facelift or skin excision.[3] A posterior neck lift paper described combining anterior platysmaplasty with anterior and lateral neck lift.[5]

A 5-year retrospective cohort compared open anterior platysmaplasty with bipolar radiofrequency-assisted liposuction in facelift patients, measuring change in cervicomental angle on photographs.[4] A deep-plane facelift surgeon has described his own 'Kelly clamp' anterior platysmaplasty variant, intended for natural, lasting results.[6]

Complications of platysmaplasty include bleeding or hematoma, infection, numbness, temporary nerve weakness, contour problems and recurrent bands; over-removal of neck fat can cause a 'cobra neck' deformity.[1] Hematoma is the most common facelift complication; a review of 1078 facelifts studied factors linked to it.[7]

Studies are surgical case series and retrospective cohorts: grade improvements in 33 patients,[3] a comparison with radiofrequency-assisted liposuction,[4] and a 10-year follow-up of identical twins operated with different facelift techniques, one including endoscopic midface lift with open anterior platysmaplasty.[8]
